Sec. 1.4 (pp. 568-570) gives five vowels, diphthongs, stop places, nasals, two sibilants, /l/, probably two rhotics, syllable types V, VR, CV, CVR (after De Hoz 2010), and stresses that the script is not fully deciphered and the language unidentified; no accent/stress statement anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent acento/acentua/prosod/tónica: zero hits).

sources.citation: Koch, John T. 2019. Common Ground and Progress on the Celtic of the South-western (SW) Inscriptions. Aberystwyth: University of Wales Centre for Advanced Welsh and Celtic Studies (Celtic Studies Publications), 131 pp. ISBN 978-1-907029-26-4.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Historical-comparative commentary under the Celtic hypothesis: treatment of Proto-Celtic diphthongs, *u̯-, *(p), b/m alternation, syncope in individual etymologies, claim that the script was borrowed from a language phonologically like Iberian/Palaeo-Basque (no /m/, no /w/ sign). The only 'accent' token (s.v. kiielaoe) concerns a reconstructed Pre-Celtic movable accent in *kéilii̯o-/*kilii̯o-, not the SW language. No statement on Tartessian word accent in 131 pp. (a full-text search for stress/accent/stress/prosod/penult/tonic).

sources.citation: Valério, Miguel. 2008. Origin and development of the Paleohispanic scripts: the orthography and phonology of the Southwestern alphabet. Revista Portuguesa de Arqueologia 11(2), 107-138.

sources.note: Derives the SW script from Phoenician; reconstructs a 29-sign system: 5 vowels, 3 stop series x 5 vowel-bound signs, 9 free consonant letters; discusses vocalic redundancy, absence of voice distinction, rare letters. No statement on stress/accent of the SW language; endnote 9 speculates that Iberian word-final stops may result from 'accent-driven loss of final vowels' (another language).

sources.note: Language section weighs the Celtic vs Anatolian vs unknown-IE hypotheses from the formula words (naŕkeenii, baare), vowel statistics (scarcity of e, frequency of a, e mostly in first syllables), and states the script renders the language 'sílaba a sílaba' through the pseudo-syllabograms; nothing on accent/stress.

sources.citation: Rodríguez Ramos, Jesús. 2000. Sobre la geminación gráfica de signos vocálicos en la escritura sudlusitano-tartesia. Veleia 17, 147-152.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The one study of the only graphic phenomenon that could in principle encode prosody (doubled vowel signs). Conclusion: two orthographic rules of some stone-cutters - a vowel is doubled before tautosyllabic r (unless preceded by a stop sign or o/u), and every absolute-final i is doubled (unless preceded by a stop sign); possibly word-initial o. Quotes Correa 1993 that doubling 'podrían deberse, tal vez, a normas gráficas desconocidas (representación de cantidad, etc.) o al encuentro de morfemas'; leaves open whether doubling before r reflects phonetic lengthening. Accent is never invoked.
